subtype: Approach: writing it down as soon as it is told [Action]
passage: Damini, look at this small diary I still keep. I'm Pankaj, and when I was ten, my teacher, Mr Kulkarni, called out what we needed for the next day's science class: a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper. Most children nodded and hoped to remember. I took out my little diary and wrote the four items at once, in a hurry, before the next lesson began. That night I checked it twice, once at dinner and once before sleep. In class, I was the only one with all four things. Writing had made my head free to think about the experiment.

qa.q: What four items did the teacher ask for?
qa.a: The teacher asked for a torch, a spoon, a small mirror and a piece of black paper.

qa.q: Why did the narrator write the items at once?
qa.a: Pankaj wanted the list safe in the diary instead of in a head that might forget, and felt sure this would help.

qa.q: What choice in the story helped the narrator have all four items, and why?
qa.a: Writing them down at once and checking twice helped, because the list stayed correct and the narrator could check it later.

qa.q: How did the other children in the class fare?
qa.a: Most children only nodded and hoped to remember, and Pankaj was the only one with all four things, so the others probably missed some items.

grounding: Pankaj writes down the items the teacher names in a small diary at once, which frees the mind from holding them and lets the list be checked later.

subtype: Approach: writing it down as soon as it is told [Action]
passage: Vandana ma'am announced tomorrow's list over the roar of the rain on the tin roof of Class 4. "Old newspaper, a plastic bottle, a sponge, two rubber bands!" Half the class didn't hear. Tushar did, and before the next word he had his little diary out on his knee. His pencil was blunt, so he wrote big: NEWSPAPER. BOTTLE. SPONGE. 2 RUBBER BANDS. When the power went out and the fans stopped, children started shouting questions at each other. Tushar didn't need to. The list was already in the diary, not in his head. That night, at home, he ticked each thing as he put it in the bag, then checked the page once more before sleeping.

qa.q: What was the noise over which Vandana ma'am announced the list?
qa.a: She announced it over the roar of the rain on the tin roof.

qa.q: How did Tushar probably feel when the other children started shouting questions?
qa.a: He probably felt calm and relieved, because the list was already written in his diary.

qa.q: What other approach might suit a child who cannot write fast enough, and why?
qa.a: That child could ask a friend to read the list back after class, because a second person catches what was missed.

qa.q: How does the noisy moment look to the classmates who did not hear the list?
qa.a: They feel confused and anxious, shouting questions at each other because they have nothing to check.

grounding: It shows a boy writing the teacher's items down immediately so he does not have to hold them in his mind and can check later.

subtype: Approach: writing it down as soon as it is told [Action]
passage: At the end of the day, Neelam ma'am called out the things for Saturday's Science practical: a lemon, salt, a steel spoon, a candle and a matchbox for her to use. Yogesh opened his pocket diary and wrote while she was still talking. By the time she said "matchbox", he had written it. On the auto ride home through the traffic near the flyover, his friends argued about whether it was lemon or orange. Yogesh just listened to the horns. His head felt light. The list was not in there any more; it was in the diary. At home he read the page to his grandmother, and together they found everything except the candle. Dadi sent him to the corner shop before it closed.

qa.q: What was the matchbox for, according to Neelam ma'am?
qa.a: The matchbox was for her to use.

qa.q: How did Yogesh feel on the auto ride while his friends argued?
qa.a: He felt light and relaxed, because the list was safely in his diary instead of in his head.

qa.q: What would help Yogesh even more when a list is long?
qa.a: He could add a tick box beside each item, because ticking while packing makes the double-check quick.

qa.q: How does Yogesh's diary look to his arguing friends?
qa.a: To his friends it would be a handy way to settle the argument, and they might wish they had written the list too.

grounding: It shows a boy writing the teacher's items down at once, freeing his mind and letting him check at home.
